title: How the World Trade Center Memorial Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant discuss the World Trade Center Memorial ahead of the tenth anniversary of September 11, 2001. They cover the original WTC complex's scale and design (exoskeleton with steel core, hat truss, sway tests), the 1993 truck bombing, the 9/11 collapses and why the towers fell, the cleanup at Ground Zero (scrap metal diversion, toxic materials, first responder illnesses, Zadroga Bill), the new Freedom Tower (One World Trade Center), and the memorial design by Michael Arad and Peter Walker (reflecting absence pools, swamp white oaks, bronze name wall), the museum underground with the Survivor Stairs and slurry wall, the controversial unidentified remains exhibit, and how to donate. Transcript is a machine-garbled text with some errors; names are spelled as the hosts give them where clear.

segments.title: Opening banter and anniversary context
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about Josh's health and the upcoming tenth anniversary of September 11, noting the memorial's dedication on September 11, 2011 and the museum expected in 2012.

segments.title: Scale of the original World Trade Center complex
segments.summary: The complex covered about sixteen acres with seven buildings, roughly 10 million square feet of office space, and about 50,000 workers plus many daily visitors. The North Tower was 1,368 feet and the South Tower slightly shorter. Each tower weighed about as much as 172,000 Ford Explorers.

segments.title: Sway tests and exoskeleton structural design
segments.summary: Designers worried about sway and had a psychologist in Eugene, Oregon test people in a swaying office building; people became dizzy and nauseated after small sways, so shock absorbers were built in. The towers used an exoskeleton of outside columns, a central steel core, and hat trusses connecting them.

segments.title: Port Authority police and the 1993 bombing
segments.summary: The complex had its own police desk, zip code and mail carriers. Lawrence Wien took out a New York Times ad warning about air hazards, and an Air Alina flight narrowly missed the North Tower. In 1993 a truck bomb of about 1,000 pounds of explosives killed six people and injured thousands.

segments.title: September 11 attacks and personal memories
segments.summary: The hosts recall September 11, 2001, when the second tower was hit and the buildings collapsed. Josh describes being stranded in Atlanta, and both reflect on how the event hit harder during recent research.

segments.title: Why the towers fell
segments.summary: The hosts explain the collapse: the planes severed thin exterior columns on the upper floors, fires weakened the steel, and the top floors fell onto lower floors in a domino effect. The towers fell nearly straight down, which the hosts note was fortunate. The North Tower collapsed into its own footprint, and Building 7 and others were destroyed.
topics: why the World Trade Center towers collapsed

segments.title: Ground Zero cleanup, toxic materials and health effects
segments.summary: About 300,000 tons of scrap metal were generated, and the mafia was caught diverting scrap to its own junkyards. Debris went to Fresh Kill Landfill under police escort. The cleanup took about nine months and came in under budget at roughly $650 million. Toxic materials included lead, cadmium, mercury, asbestos and other contaminants, and many first responders became sick. A $625 million settlement and the Zadroga Bill were discussed, with cancer not included in the bill.

segments.title: One World Trade Center and earlier memorials
segments.summary: The hosts discuss criticism of the new One World Trade Center, originally called the Freedom Tower, and its design by Daniel Libeskind. They also mention earlier memorials including the Sphere by Fritz Koenig and the Tribute in Light.

segments.title: Memorial design: Reflecting Absence, swamp white oaks, museum, and remains exhibit
segments.summary: The memorial design by Michael Arad, a Georgia Tech alumnus, won a 2003 competition of 5,201 entries from 63 countries. Its two reflecting pools sit in the old footprints, with swamp white oaks on a suspended paving system, a bronze name wall, and a glass pavilion with the surviving tridents. The underground museum includes the Survivor Stairs and a slurry wall section. A controversial plan would display unidentified human remains, and the hosts discuss donation options.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close with a listener mail address and a plug for a video podcast.
